distinguishing_feature: Acute vaginitis has sudden onset over days; chronic vaginitis has symptoms persisting beyond ~4 weeks or recurring
Atrophic vaginitis occurs in postmenopausal women with low estrogen, typically dryness rather than infective discharge
Postpartum timing (within 6 weeks of delivery) distinguishes vaginitis following delivery
Herpesviral cervicitis classically presents with painful vesicles/ulcers; gonococcal cervicitis presents with mucopurulent discharge without ulceration
Postpartum timing distinguishes cervicitis following delivery from a primary STI-related cervicitis
Superficial dyspareunia is pain at the vaginal entry/introitus, typically on initial penetration
Deep dyspareunia is pain felt internally/deep in the pelvis, often with deep thrusting
Deep dyspareunia suggests pelvic pathology (endometriosis, PID); superficial dyspareunia suggests vulvovaginal/introital causes
Diagnosis of exclusion after a known physiological/substance-related cause has been ruled out, unlike other specified dyspareunia with an identified physical cause
Other vulvodynia has an identified subtype/pattern documented; unspecified vulvodynia lacks further characterization
Vulvodynia is primarily a pain/burning syndrome; pruritus vulvae is primarily itch-driven
Acute vulvitis has sudden onset; chronic vulvitis persists or recurs beyond the acute phase
Pruritus vulvae is itch without necessarily visible inflammation; chronic vulvitis shows ongoing inflammatory changes on exam

Primary dysmenorrhea has no identifiable pelvic pathology and typically starts near menarche; secondary dysmenorrhea is due to an underlying condition (e.g. endometriosis, fibroids) and often starts later with worsening pain
Primary dysmenorrhea has been specifically confirmed to have no underlying pathology, unlike unspecified dysmenorrhea where this hasn't been established
Cycle regularity distinguishes these — regular cycle length vs irregular/unpredictable cycle length
Timing at puberty (often anovulatory, self-limiting) distinguishes this from established irregular heavy bleeding in adulthood
Primary amenorrhea = menstruation never started by age 15 (or 13 with no breast development); secondary amenorrhea = previously menstruating, now absent for 3+ cycles or 6 months
Primary amenorrhea specifically confirms menstruation never occurred, unlike unspecified amenorrhea where primary vs secondary hasn't been established
Secondary amenorrhea specifically confirms a prior menstrual history before cessation
Primary oligomenorrhea = infrequent periods since menarche; secondary oligomenorrhea = previously normal cycles that became infrequent
Primary oligomenorrhea specifically confirms the pattern has been present since menarche
Tubal origin relates to tubal patency/damage (e.g. prior PID); uterine origin relates to cavity abnormalities (e.g. fibroids, polyps, adhesions)
Anovulation shows irregular/absent ovulation on cycle tracking; tubal origin shows normal ovulation but blocked/damaged tubes on imaging
Unspecified infertility has not yet been attributed to a specific origin, unlike 'other origin' where a cause outside tubal/uterine/anovulatory has been identified
Male infertility unspecified is coded for the male patient directly; the encounter code is used when documenting male-factor infertility in the female partner's own record
Galactorrhea is specifically milky bilateral discharge unrelated to childbirth; nipple discharge is a broader category covering any discharge type/color, often unilateral
Abnormal uterine/vaginal bleeding is the broader bleeding-pattern code; irregular menstruation unspecified emphasizes cycle-timing irregularity specifically
